name: HR's role in today's organizations
origin: Session 1 · Strategic business partner vs employee advocate
purpose: What does HR do – and for whom? HR has to serve the business and the employees at the same time.

parts.label: Administrative activities
points: Must work, but creates little advantage

parts.label: Operational activities
points: Running the HR practices: hiring, training, appraisal, pay rounds

parts.label: Transformational activities
points: Strategic HRM: aligning people with strategy, change, culture

parts.label: Strategic business partner
points: Speaks the language of the business

parts.label: Employee advocate
points: Protects employees' interests, well-being and fairness

apply: Classify what HR does in the case: administrative, operational or transformational?
Check whose interests the HR decision serves – business partner, employee advocate, or both?
Remember: HRM is done by ALL managers, not only by the HR department – look at the line manager in the case
pitfalls: Treating partner and advocate as either/or – the course frames them as two sides of one role
example: Student metaphors from the first class: functional, people focus/support, team, system (chess), nurturer (gardener), strategic organizer, “invisible hand” (iceberg: manage values, culture, attitudes below the surface).

name: The individual human resource cycle
purpose: Which HR practices does an employee go through – and how do they connect? It is also the map of this course.
apply: Locate the case problem in the cycle (e.g. a pay problem that is really a performance-management problem)
Trace the knock-on effects: a change in one practice affects the others (PRP depends on PM)
Do not forget employer branding upstream of staffing
pitfalls: Looking at one practice in isolation – the practices must fit together (horizontal fit)
example: Course structure: recruitment & selection → performance management → rewards & compensation → employer branding.

name: Why bother about HRM?
purpose: Why do people practices matter for performance and beyond?

parts.label: Human capital theory (HCT)
points: Skills and knowledge are an investment

parts.label: Resource-based view (RBV)
points: People and their capabilities can be valuable, rare, hard to imitate

parts.label: Well-being impact
points: HR decisions have effects outside the firm

apply: Justify an HR investment with HCT (return on skills) or RBV (hard-to-imitate people capabilities)
Add the well-being lens: what does the decision do to employees and society?
pitfalls: Arguing only with costs – the course frames HR as a source of value
example: HR Director exercise: fast-fashion firm, 10,000 employees, CEO wants −12 % labour cost AND sustainability leadership – choose two of six options.

name: From “control” to “commitment”
origin: Evolution of core principles · Walton-style contrast
purpose: How does HRM create value – by controlling people or by gaining their commitment?

parts.label: Control
points: Close monitoring, precise and narrow job descriptions
Value = minimize labour cost, maximize output
Bentham's Panopticon, Ford assembly line; today: call centres, chicken factories

parts.label: Commitment
points: Success depends on securing commitment, not control
Committed workforce goes the extra mile

apply: Diagnose where the case firm sits: monitoring and piece rates (control) or trust, teams, development (commitment)?
Ask what the work needs: routine, easily measured tasks vs knowledge work and innovation
Link to PM and rewards: control → narrow metrics, individual PRP; commitment → development, collective rewards
pitfalls: Assuming control is always “bad” – the problem is its side effects (stress, no extra mile, “not my job”)
Forgetting the evidence: Japanese plants in North America almost matched Japan
example: Womack et al. (1990): hours per vehicle – Japanese plants in Japan 16.8 on average, US plants in North America 24.9, Japanese plants in North America 20.9. The management model travels.

name: Universalism: best practice
origin: Pfeffer (1998) – “Building profits by putting people first”
purpose: Is there one set of HR practices that works everywhere?

parts.label: Employment security
points: People share ideas without fearing for their job

parts.label: High pay contingent on company performance

apply: Use the seven practices as a checklist to audit the case firm
Then challenge it with best fit: does each practice fit this firm's strategy and context?
pitfalls: Applying the list blindly – contingency scholars argue context decides

name: Best practice vs best fit
origin: Pfeffer (1998) vs Jackson & Schuler (1984); Paauwe & Farndale (2017)
purpose: Should a firm copy universal HR practices or design practices that fit its context?

parts.label: Best practice (universalism)
points: One bundle of HR practices improves performance everywhere

parts.label: Best fit (contingency)
points: “Matching model”: tight fit between HR and context
Most effective way of managing varies with the organisation's context

apply: Describe the context: strategy, workforce, labour market, country, unions, technology
Explain why a practice that works elsewhere (e.g. London office, another country) may not fit here
Recommend: keep universal principles (fairness, clear criteria) but adapt the design
pitfalls: Copy-pasting one site's practices to all sites (e.g. National Office Supplies wanting standard practices)
example: Inditex: the same firm, but positions in different countries need different recruitment strategies.

name: The Harvard Model
origin: Beer et al. (1984) – Map of the HRM territory
purpose: How do stakeholders and context shape HR policy choices – and what long-term consequences follow?

parts.label: Situational factors
points: Workforce characteristics, business strategy and conditions
Task technology, laws and societal values

apply: List the stakeholders in the case and what each wants
List the situational factors that constrain the choice
Classify the proposed policy (influence, flow, rewards, work systems)
Predict the 4 Cs and the long-term consequences – including feedback loops back to stakeholders
pitfalls: Forgetting the feedback loops (dashed arrows): consequences change stakeholder interests and the situation
Ignoring non-shareholder stakeholders – the model is a stakeholder model
